subject: Culture
title: Naming Taboos
description: A fast breakdown of Naming Taboos for builders.

hook.text: In China, naming a child after a living elder is disrespectful. In the West, it's an honor.

buildup.text: Many cultures believe a name carries power. Saying a dead person's name can disturb their spirit.

discovery.text: Some Aboriginal Australian groups stop using a deceased person's name entirely for years.

twist.text: Ancient Egyptians believed erasing a name from monuments destroyed the person's afterlife.

climax.text: Names aren't just labels. In many traditions, they're vessels of identity, fate, and memory.

punchline.text: A name can be a gift, a weapon, or a prayer.

quiz.question: In traditional Chinese culture, naming a child after a living elder is considered what?

details.summary: Many cultures treat names as possessing spiritual power, making certain naming practices taboo. Some forbid naming children after living relatives, others prohibit speaking the names of the dead. In China, using characters from an emperor's name was once punishable by death.
details.whyItMatters: Naming taboos reveal how deeply cultures connect language to spiritual reality. They show that names are never just labels — they carry power, memory, and social obligation.
takeaways: Some cultures forbid naming children after living relatives
Aboriginal Australians may avoid names of recently deceased people
Imperial China prohibited using characters from the emperor's name

faq.question: Why do some cultures avoid the names of dead people?
faq.answer: In many Aboriginal Australian, some Native American, and certain African cultures, speaking a deceased person's name is believed to disturb their spirit or cause them pain. The name may be replaced with a description or the person simply not mentioned.

faq.question: Why was using an emperor's name characters taboo in China?
faq.answer: Chinese 'name taboo' (bìhuì) required avoiding the characters in an emperor's or ancestor's name in writing and speech. This showed respect and maintained social hierarchy. People changed their own names to avoid overlap, and texts were edited to replace forbidden characters.
